explanation: It is the only move that shifts two of a player's pieces at once. A king may not castle out of check, through check, into check or after it has moved.

claims.text: Castling moves the king and a rook in the same turn.
En passant is a pawn capture, promotion turns a pawn into another piece, and a fianchetto develops a bishop; none of them moves the king and a rook together.
Castling is the only chess move in which a player moves two pieces.
A king may not castle while in check, across or onto a square attacked by an enemy piece, or after it has moved.

evidence.restatement: Castling moves the king two squares towards a rook and puts that rook on the square the king crossed.
En passant is a pawn capture, promotion replaces a pawn, and a fianchetto develops a bishop; none moves king and rook together.
Castling is the only move in which a player moves two of their own pieces.

evidence.restatement: A king may not castle out of, through or into check, or once the king (or that rook) has moved.
Castling moves the king two squares and brings a rook across it in the same turn.
En passant is a pawn capture, promotion replaces a pawn, and a fianchetto is a bishop's development pattern; none moves king and rook together.
Castling is the only chess move in which a side moves two pieces.
Castling is barred if the king has moved, is in check, or crosses or lands on an attacked square (and if the rook has moved).
